body:
Why different cloud service models exist

Some organisations want complete software that is ready to use. Others want to develop their own software but do not want to manage the underlying operating system. Still others need control over virtual computers and installed software. Cloud service models describe these different levels of service and responsibility.

NIST identifies 3 main service models: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS) and Software as a Service (SaaS). They differ principally in what the provider supplies and what the consumer manages.

Infrastructure as a Service: IaaS

IaaS supplies fundamental computing resources such as virtual computing capacity, storage and networking. The consumer can install and operate software, including an operating system and applications, on the provisioned resources.

For example, an organisation may rent a virtual computer from a cloud provider, install its preferred operating system and run a web application. The organisation normally manages the guest operating system, its updates, applications and associated configurations. The cloud provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

IaaS offers comparatively greater control, but that control brings greater responsibility for the software installed and maintained by the consumer.

Platform as a Service: PaaS

PaaS supplies an application-hosting environment in which the consumer can deploy an application without managing the underlying physical servers or the platform's operating-system infrastructure.

For example, a college may create an online admission application and deploy it to a managed application platform. The college remains responsible for its application's logic, content and appropriate settings, while the platform provider manages the underlying environment required to run it.

PaaS is therefore particularly useful when an organisation wants to develop and operate its own application while avoiding much of the routine infrastructure management.

Software as a Service: SaaS

SaaS supplies a complete application that users can access through a browser or another compatible interface. The provider operates the application and underlying infrastructure. The user generally manages their own content, access settings and permitted application preferences rather than administering servers.

Examples include a hosted email service, an online document-editing application or a managed school-administration platform. The essential fact is that the consumer uses a completed software service, rather than building and hosting the software from the beginning.

Comparing the service models

ModelWhat the consumer receivesWhat the consumer mainly manages
IaaSVirtual computing, storage and networking resourcesOperating system, installed applications and relevant configurations
PaaSManaged environment for deploying applicationsApplication code, data and permitted application settings
SaaSReady-to-use hosted applicationOwn content, users and permitted service settings

These are broad models. Individual services may divide operational responsibilities differently, so exact contractual responsibilities should not be assumed solely from a product's marketing name.

Applying the distinction to a government office

Suppose a district office needs a digital system to receive public applications.

  • If it subscribes to an existing hosted application, it is using a SaaS-type service.
  • If its developers create a custom application and deploy it to a managed cloud platform, it is using a PaaS-type service.
  • If its technical team provisions virtual machines, installs operating systems and operates the custom application, it is using an IaaS-type service.

The same basic public-service objective can therefore be achieved using different cloud service models. The correct classification depends on the service actually provided and the responsibilities retained by the office.

India's MeghRaj initiative

GI Cloud, commonly called MeghRaj, is a Government of India cloud-computing initiative intended to accelerate the delivery of electronic government services and improve the use of ICT infrastructure. The National Informatics Centre's National Cloud services include IaaS, PaaS and SaaS offerings.

MeghRaj is an example of cloud computing being applied to government services. It is not a separate fourth service model alongside IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

Prelims focus

  • IaaS: fundamental computing resources; consumer can manage operating systems and applications.
  • PaaS: managed platform for deploying consumer-created applications.
  • SaaS: complete provider-operated application for users.
  • NIST identifies 3 principal cloud service models.
  • GI Cloud or MeghRaj is associated with Government of India cloud services.
  • Trap: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS describe the type of service, not whether a cloud is public, private or hybrid.

[Sources: NIST, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, SP 800-145, September 2011, sec. 2, 'Service Models', printed pp. 2–3, consulted 4 November 2026; National Informatics Centre, 'National Cloud', MeghRaj and IaaS/PaaS/SaaS service descriptions, consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The service model depends on whether the consumer needs infrastructure, an application platform or ready-made software.

title: Cloud Service Models: Understanding IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

body:
Service model and deployment model answer different questions

Cloud service models describe what type of computing service is supplied. Cloud deployment models describe for whom the cloud infrastructure is organised and how it is made available.

The same type of application may run in different deployment environments. For example, an organisation may run its own application on a public cloud platform or on a private cloud reserved for that organisation. A deployment model does not automatically determine whether the application is IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.

Public cloud

A public cloud is cloud infrastructure made available for open use by the general public. The infrastructure may be operated by a commercial company, an academic organisation or another qualifying provider.

Different customers can use resources from a common infrastructure while appropriate controls separate their accounts, applications and data. The model offers access to shared capacity without requiring each customer to build a complete data centre.

The word public describes the availability of the cloud service to potential customers. It does not mean that every customer's files, passwords or databases are publicly visible.

Private cloud

A private cloud is provided for the exclusive use of a single organisation. Different departments or units within that organisation may share the infrastructure.

Private-cloud infrastructure may be operated by the organisation itself, by an outside provider or through a combination of arrangements. Under the NIST definition, it may be located on the organisation's premises or elsewhere.

A private cloud may be chosen when an organisation requires particular control over computing arrangements, internal processes or access. However, a private cloud is not automatically secure simply because it is private. Security depends on proper design, management and controls.

Hybrid cloud

A hybrid cloud combines 2 or more distinct cloud infrastructures, such as private and public clouds, that remain separate but are connected by technology enabling useful interaction, such as data or application portability.

For example, an organisation may keep a sensitive records system on a private cloud while using a public cloud to supply additional capacity for a public-facing application during periods of heavy demand. Such an arrangement requires suitable connections, access controls and integration.

Merely purchasing services from 2 separate providers does not automatically create a well-integrated hybrid cloud. The defining idea is that separate cloud environments operate together for a useful purpose.

Comparison of the 3 main deployment choices

DeploymentWho uses the infrastructure?Defining feature
Public cloudAvailable to the general public as potential consumersShared provider infrastructure with customer separation
Private cloudOne organisation exclusivelyInfrastructure reserved for a single organisation
Hybrid cloudConsumers of connected distinct cloud environmentsIntegrated use of 2 or more separate clouds

NIST also identifies a community cloud for organisations with shared concerns. Its recognition explains why the NIST definition refers to 4 deployment models, even though the central comparisons here are public, private and hybrid clouds.

Cloud security is a shared responsibility

The cloud provider is responsible for the parts of the service it operates, while the consumer must manage responsibilities retained under the chosen model. These often include user permissions, accurate information handling and safe application configuration.

A public cloud can use strong protection, and a private cloud can still suffer data loss or unauthorised access. Security and privacy cannot be judged reliably from the deployment label alone.

Prelims focus

  • Public cloud infrastructure is available for use by the general public as customers.
  • Private cloud infrastructure is reserved for one organisation.
  • A private cloud may be located on or off the organisation's premises.
  • Hybrid cloud combines distinct cloud infrastructures through meaningful integration.
  • NIST recognises 4 deployment models, including community cloud.
  • Trap: Public cloud does not mean publicly accessible user data; hybrid cloud is not a synonym for any use of 2 unrelated services.

[Sources: NIST, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, SP 800-145, September 2011, sec. 2, 'Deployment Models', printed p. 3, consulted 4 November 2026; NIST, 'Cloud Computing' project overview, deployment-model summary, updated 14 September 2026, consulted 4 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A controlled connection links a government's private records cloud to a distinct public cloud with a public-facing app and extra capacity during heavy demand.
pictures.caption: A hybrid cloud connects distinct cloud environments while retaining their separate roles.

title: Public, Private and Hybrid Clouds: Where Computing Resources Are Organised

body:
Why applications need a suitable running environment

A software application needs more than its visible screens. It may depend on particular software libraries, settings and operating-system facilities. Differences between computers can sometimes make an application difficult to move or run consistently.

Containers and serverless computing are 2 approaches used to simplify application delivery and operation. They solve different problems and should not be treated as synonyms.

What is a software container?

An application container packages an application together with the software components it needs to run in a suitable compatible environment. Containers help developers deploy applications consistently across supported computers and cloud platforms.

Containers commonly share the host operating system's kernel, the central part of the operating system that manages essential computing resources. Different containers can run separate applications while relying on the same underlying kernel.

Containerisation is often described as a form of operating-system-level virtualisation.

Container versus virtual machine

A virtual machine (VM) provides a virtual computer environment with its own guest operating system. It uses virtualised computing resources supplied by the underlying infrastructure.

A typical container does not require a separate full guest operating system for each container. Instead, containers share a compatible host kernel. This can make them relatively lightweight, although the actual resource use depends on the application and platform.

Containers and VMs can be used together. For example, a cloud provider may run containers inside virtual machines. A container is therefore not necessarily an alternative to every form of virtualisation.

Advantages and limits of containers

  • Consistency: an application's required software components can be packaged together.
  • Deployment: packaged applications can be started and updated more systematically.
  • Resource efficiency: sharing an operating-system kernel can reduce some overhead compared with separately running complete guest operating systems.

Containers do not make an application automatically secure. They still require suitable permissions, secure software components and careful configuration. A container may also depend on external databases or platform-specific services, which can limit its portability.

What is serverless computing?

Serverless computing is a model in which the service provider takes responsibility for much of the underlying server provisioning and routine operational management. The application developer or consumer concentrates more directly on code, application behaviour and permitted configuration.

The name is potentially misleading: serverless does not mean that no servers exist. Physical servers still execute the work; the consumer generally does not manage them directly.

Function as a Service

A familiar serverless pattern is Function as a Service (FaaS). A function is a small unit of application work that can run in response to an event.

For example, a student may upload an application form. The upload event may trigger a function that checks basic file details and records that the document arrived. The platform starts the required computing work and can adjust the resources provided as the number of events changes.

Serverless services commonly use usage-related charging models. However, their exact cost structures and limits differ. An event-driven function is not automatically free, and frequent use may produce significant charges.

Containers, serverless and cloud service models

Containers describe a way to package and run applications. Serverless describes an approach to providing and managing execution resources. IaaS, PaaS and SaaS describe service responsibilities. These classifications are related but do not answer the same question.

A serverless platform may use containers internally. A developer may run containers on IaaS virtual machines or use a managed container platform. The correct description depends on the actual service and who manages each part.

Prelims focus

  • Containers package applications and their dependencies for supported execution environments.
  • Containers commonly share the host operating-system kernel.
  • A virtual machine normally runs a guest operating system.
  • Serverless reduces direct server-management responsibilities for the consumer.
  • Function as a Service can execute code in response to events.
  • Trap: Serverless systems still use servers, and containers are not automatically secure or completely portable.

[Sources: NIST, Application Container Security Guide, SP 800-190, September 2017, abstract and application-container concepts, consulted 4 November 2026; Cloud Native Computing Foundation, Cloud Native Glossary, entries 'Serverless' and 'Containers', consulted 4 November 2026; NIST, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, SP 800-145, September 2011, sec. 2, service-model definitions.]
